prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The map places the camera wearer’s hands, forearms, knees, and lower torso in the near field, roughly 0.2–0.8 m away, while the pale wall or board across the upper part of the strip is about 0.5–1.5 m ahead and the ground beyond it is farther away. No separate person is clearly resolved: the visible body regions belong predominantly to the wearer, and no face is available for determining facing direction or gaze. Across the five frames, one arm moves very close to the camera in frame 2, retreats or drops partly out of view in frame 3, extends forward in frame 4, and the hand and cord approach the upper-right near field in frame 5; these items remain within the wearer’s arm’s reach. Depth ordering and limb occlusion are clearer than in RGB, but metric distances are only rough because brightness is not calibrated, the pale wall merges with near limbs, dark regions may mean either distant or failed depth, and boundaries around the thin cord and overlapping body parts are unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The masks separate several visible regions of the camera wearer—hands or arms above, legs and torso below—from the black background, making their left/right placement and overlap easier to follow than in RGB. The large person masks lie within roughly 0.2–1 m of the camera and overlap one another because they are parts of the same nearby wearer; no clearly distinct second person, face orientation, or gaze direction is recoverable despite multiple person labels. The labelled kite in frame 1 is high and slightly left, roughly 1–2 m away, while a surfboard-labelled region appears low-right in frame 2, but both identifications are spatially uncertain and the latter conflicts with the RGB appearance. Over time, the segmented arm shifts from left/central in frame 1 to very close and central in frame 2, becomes fragmented in frame 3, extends across the centre-right in frame 4, and forms a large partly out-of-view mask on the right in frame 5; masks reveal occlusion extents but are unreliable where limbs, clothing, cord, and background merge.
descriptions.pose: The pose map isolates only a few articulated structures: a magenta hand skeleton appears left of centre in frame 1, a yellow upper-limb chain with overlapping magenta hand landmarks appears centre-right in frame 4, and a close magenta hand appears near the upper-right in frame 5. These joints correspond to the camera wearer’s limbs at approximately 0.2–0.8 m, all within the wearer’s reach, with the frame-4 arm extending forward and right and the frame-5 hand moving closer to the camera; no separate person-to-person distance can be established. Most of the wearer’s body, all faces, and frames 2–3 are undetected, so body facing, gaze, and whether anyone looks toward the wearer cannot be determined. The skeleton makes joint direction and hand-over-arm overlap clearer than RGB, but it is unreliable for occluded or cropped limbs, sometimes omits visible joints entirely, and the dense frame-5 hand landmarks may include errors caused by the blue cord and partial view.
